title: Generalized Planning with Deep Reinforcement Learning
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of generalized planning: learning a policy from small planning instances that can be reused to solve much larger instances in the same domain. The authors argue that a good generalized planner should discover principles that extend beyond the training distribution, rather than memorizing instance-specific solutions.

The proposed approach combines graph neural networks with deep reinforcement learning. Planning states are represented as graphs derived from PDDL predicates, and candidate actions are represented through their effects. A policy and value function are trained with PPO on sparse binary rewards, using randomly generated instances from five classical planning domains: Blocksworld, Satellite, Logistics, Gripper, and Ferry. During inference, the learned policy is optionally embedded in a GBFS-style search procedure (GBFS-GNN) to improve performance on harder instances.

The paper evaluates whether policies trained on small instances can generalize to much larger ones. The main findings are that the approach generalizes well on four of the five domains and can outperform or match a strong classical planner on several metrics, but it fails to generalize well in Logistics. The work is methodological and does not involve teachers, students, or educational settings; it is included here only because it relates to generative/AI methods, not because it studies instructional coaching or lesson feedback.

identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring / automated planning or decision-support system archetype that learns policies to choose actions in sequential decision problems.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies generalized planning policies learned with deep reinforcement learning and graph neural networks for classical planning domains, not an educational product or teacher-facing tool.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/algorithmic machine learning paper on generalized planning in classical AI domains, with no educational intervention, no teacher sample, and no empirical study of a K-12 instructional coaching tool.
impact_tier_rationale: There are no reported education outcomes, no effect sizes, and no evidence of impact on teachers, coaching, or lesson-plan feedback in K–12 settings.
